title: Tinder
brief: Design a system like Tinder: you see a stack of nearby people one card at a time and swipe right to like or left to pass. When two people have both liked each other it is a match, and they can chat. The hard parts are picking good nearby cards, taking a huge stream of swipes, and spotting a match the instant it happens.

functional: Show a stack of nearby people who fit my filters (age, distance, gender).
Swipe right to like or left to pass on a card.
Never show me the same person twice.
Detect a match when both people have liked each other.
Tell both people about the match, and open a chat.
Update my location as I move.

nonFunctional.name: Swipe latency
nonFunctional.target: A swipe is accepted in under 100 ms at the 99th percentile

nonFunctional.name: Match speed
nonFunctional.target: A match shows on the swiping screen at once, and the other person is told within 5 seconds

nonFunctional.name: Card load
nonFunctional.target: The next stack loads in under 300 ms

nonFunctional.name: No repeats
nonFunctional.target: A person I already swiped is shown again almost never (under 1 in 10,000 cards)

nonFunctional.name: Durability
nonFunctional.target: A right swipe is never lost, or a match could be missed

outOfScope: Chat itself (reuse the Chat System design)

estimate.note: Assumptions, not facts: a swipe is one small write, peak is about 3 times the average, and the seen filter uses a fixed number of bits per swipe. Swipes per second drive the write path, the seen set drives memory.

inputs.label: Share of swipes that are right swipes
Right swipes that complete a match
Bloom filter bits per person seen
inputs.note: About 10 bits gives roughly 1% false positives.

outputs.label: Swipes per second at peak
outputs.note: Evenings and weekends in busy cities.

outputs.label: Match lookups per second at peak
outputs.note: Only right swipes need to ask: did they like me first?

outputs.label: People in one user's seen set

api.does: Returns the next cards: nearby people who fit my filters, ranked, never seen.
Records a like or pass. swipeId makes a retry safe. Replies with match: true if it completes a match.
Updates my position in the geo index.
Lists my matches, each with a chat id.
Undo the last swipe. Often a paid feature.

data.fields: userId, name, age, photos, bio, prefs, lastActive
data.store: Document or key-value store keyed by userId.
data.why: Read by id when cards are built. No joins, so it shards cleanly.
The durable log of every choice. It is write-heavy and only read back by one user.

data.fields: targetId to set of likerIds (right swipes only)
data.store: In-memory key-value store, sharded by targetId.
data.why: Answers 'did B like A?' with one lookup at swipe time. Only likes go in, which is a small share of swipes.

data.store: In-memory store, one Bloom filter per user.
data.why: Tests 'did I already swipe this person?' in memory, at a few bits per person.

evolution.title: One server, one database
evolution.problem: Start with what works for a small town: all profiles in one table, and the app asks for people who fit the filters.
evolution.change: The API server runs a SQL query for profiles within a distance and the user's filters, and returns a page of cards.

evolution.title: A geo index for candidates
evolution.problem: Distance on raw latitude and longitude means scanning every user, and locations change all day. At 10M users in a metro area the query takes seconds.
evolution.change: Keep an in-memory geo index: the map is cut into cells and each cell lists the people in it. A deck query reads the user's cell and its neighbours, then filters by preferences. It is the nearby search building block, shown as one node.

evolution.title: Record swipes and find matches
evolution.problem: Nothing remembers a choice yet. Without it there are no matches, and cards repeat.
evolution.change: A swipe service writes each swipe to a swipe log. On a right swipe from A to B it reads whether B already liked A. If yes, it creates a match. Writes and reads both hit the one log.

evolution.title: Rank the candidates
evolution.problem: Sorting by distance shows the same few people to everyone nearby. Popular profiles get swamped, and others are never seen.
evolution.change: A ranker scores the geo candidates with a few signals (activity, mutual preferences, past likes) and returns the best. It loads profiles for the cards it keeps.
evolution.numbers: Cards ranked per deck, about 20 out of a few hundred

evolution.title: Never show someone twice
evolution.problem: Each user swipes about 36,500 people in a year. Checking every candidate against the swipe log is a database read per card, and users hate repeats.
evolution.change: Keep a Bloom filter per user in memory. The ranker drops candidates the filter says were seen, and the swipe service adds each new swipe to it (later via the queue). A rare false positive just hides one person, which is harmless.
evolution.numbers: the estimator shows the filter size per user

evolution.title: Swipes at very high write rate
evolution.problem: Peak swipes are over 100K per second. The match check must be a fast lookup, and the durable log cannot take a synchronous write for every swipe.
evolution.change: Right swipes go into a likes index keyed by the target, so 'did B like A?' is one in-memory read. The swipe is also put on a queue. Its consumer writes the swipe log in batches and updates the seen filter, so bursts do not hit the database.
evolution.numbers: the estimator shows swipes and lookups per second

evolution.title: Hand off to chat and notify
evolution.problem: A match is only useful if both people know, and can talk.
evolution.change: On a match the swipe service creates the chat through the Chat System block and sends a push through notifications to the person who is offline. The swiper sees the match in the swipe reply.

steps.say: I swipe right on Sam. The app posts the swipe with a swipe id it made itself.
The API passes it to the swipe service.
The service asks the likes index: has Sam already liked me? It also adds my like of Sam, in that order.
It puts the swipe on the queue. A consumer will write it to the swipe log in a batch.
The queue consumer appends the swipe to the durable log.
It also marks Sam as seen in my Bloom filter.
Sam had liked me, so it is a match. The service creates the chat.
It tells Sam by push. My screen already shows 'It is a match' from the reply.
I open the app. It sends my location and filters.
The API asks the geo index for people in my cell and the cells around it.
It gets a few hundred user ids and checks them against my filters.
The ranker takes the candidates to order them.
It drops everyone my Bloom filter says I have already swiped.
It reads the profiles of the best 20 and the deck goes back to the phone.

deepDives.title: Detecting a match at swipe time
deepDives.question: How do we know, within one request, that the other person already liked me?

options.name: Query the swipe log
options.pros: No extra system. The log already has the answer.
options.cons: The log is partitioned by swiper, so 'who swiped me' is a scatter across partitions. Too slow for every swipe.

options.name: Likes index keyed by target
options.pros: One in-memory lookup per right swipe. Only likes are stored, a small share of all swipes.
options.cons: A second copy of the data. It must be rebuilt from the log if lost.

options.name: Scan on a timer
options.cons: The match shows up minutes late and kills the moment. Not acceptable.

deepDives.pick: Likes index keyed by target, rebuilt from the log
deepDives.because: A match needs a fast reverse lookup, and that is a different access path from the log. Write my like first, then read theirs. If both swipe at once, at least one of us sees the other. A pair key makes the match idempotent.

deepDives.title: Remembering who I have seen
deepDives.question: How do we avoid repeats without a database read per card?

options.name: Exact set in the database
options.pros: No false positives. Easy to reason about.
options.cons: A read per candidate, and tens of thousands of rows per user. Heavy and slow.

options.name: Bloom filter in memory
options.pros: About 10 bits per person. A test is constant time and needs no disk.
options.cons: A small false-positive rate hides a few unseen people. Cannot remove entries, so undo needs care.

options.name: Exact set plus Bloom in front
options.pros: Bloom says 'definitely new' fast, and the exact set settles the rest.
options.cons: More moving parts. The exact set is still read for many cards.

deepDives.pick: Bloom filter per user, rebuilt from the swipe log
deepDives.because: Hiding one person in a hundred is a fine price in a pool of thousands. If a filter fills up or an undo is needed, rebuild it from the log. For the exact answer, the log is still the truth.

deepDives.title: Building the deck
deepDives.question: Query on every card, or prepare a batch ahead?

options.name: Query on demand
options.pros: Always fresh. Reflects my newest location and filters.
options.cons: Every swipe cycle costs a geo read, a ranking pass and a profile fetch.

options.name: Precompute a batch
options.pros: Take 20 or so cards per request. Ranking cost is spread, and the next swipe is instant.
options.cons: Cards can go stale: people leave the area or go offline. Need a refresh rule.

deepDives.pick: Precompute about 20 cards, refresh when low or moved
deepDives.because: Users swipe fast and cards load from the phone's own stack. Staleness is tolerable, and the seen filter still runs on each refresh.

failures.what: Two people swipe right at the same moment
failures.impact: Each checks the likes index before the other's like lands, so neither sees a match and it is lost.
failures.fix: Write my like first, then read theirs. Whoever is second always sees the first. Create the match by a pair key so a double detection is harmless.

failures.impact: Match lookups fail for the users on that shard, so matches are missed.
failures.fix: Replicate the index, and rebuild a shard from the swipe log. While rebuilding, fall back to a slower log lookup for those users.

failures.impact: Swipes are not yet in the log, so the seen filter and match history lag. A person can reappear.
failures.fix: The swipe service writes the likes index itself, before the queue, so matches stay correct. The phone also remembers its recent swipes and hides them. Scale consumers on queue depth.

failures.impact: No decks are built, so users see a blank screen.
failures.fix: Fall back to distance order from the geo index with the seen filter. Serve the last good deck from a cache. Time out the ranker at a short limit.

failures.impact: One geo cell has millions of people and a single node cannot serve it.
failures.fix: Split dense cells into smaller ones and replicate the hot ones. Sample candidates instead of listing all.

scaling.limit: Seen filters are the largest memory cost, growing with swipes per user times days kept
scaling.lever: Cap the window, drop filters of inactive users and rebuild them on return, and shard by userId. Lower bits per entry if more false positives are fine.

scaling.limit: Swipes at peak need a very high write rate
scaling.lever: Partition the queue and log by swiper id. Batch writes. The match path only uses memory, so it is not limited by the log.

scaling.limit: Dense places make geo cells hot
scaling.lever: Use finer cells in dense areas and cache their candidate lists for short periods. Pick candidates by sampling.

recap.key: A deck is geo candidates, ranked and filtered by a per-user Bloom filter. A match is one reverse lookup in a likes index at swipe time, with the durable log written behind a queue.
recap.numbers: For 50M daily users at 100 swipes each: about 58K swipes per second on average and 174K at peak, around 52K match lookups per second at peak, and about 45 KB of Bloom filter per user.
moves: Find candidates from a geo index, then rank them
Check the reverse like in memory, write the log behind a queue
Use a Bloom filter per user so nobody repeats
Hand a match to chat and notifications as single blocks
